solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Made a nuisance of oneself with Poles in a hostile place

indicators.note: the phrase for misbehaving is read as carrying the compass points along with it, holding them in its middle

parts.note: 'was a pest', with the article dropped
South and North, the two poles

explanation.surface: Someone who kept pestering people, together with some Poles, ended up somewhere unfriendly.
explanation.walkthrough: The poles sit inside WAS PEST to make WASPS NEST; the nuisance-making links neatly to the stinging insects.
explanation.definitionFit: A nest full of angry stinging insects is the stock image of a dangerous spot to stumble into.

clue.text: Why cut across desert in great heat?

indicators.note: cutting a word shortens it, so its final letter is lost
lying across something means stretching around it on both sides

parts.note: the word 'why' with its last letter removed
to rat is to desert or betray one's side

explanation.surface: A question about why anyone would trek across a desert in blistering heat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Desert' looks like sand, but it is the verb: to rat on someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Wrath is fierce anger, and heat is a common figure for passionate temper, so great heat suits it.

clue.text: Smart newspaper, working to cover book and film

indicators.note: covering something means wrapping around it, so the word for working goes round the next items

parts.note: a Sunday is a weekend newspaper
a machine that is going is working
a tome is a large book

explanation.surface: A smartly produced paper whose staff are busy covering both a book and a film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smart' looks like praise for the paper; it is the definition, describing best church-going clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunday-go-to-meeting clothes are the best outfit kept for church, so the phrase describes dressing smartly.

clue.text: Pupil seen initially sometime after nine, Thursday

indicators.note: after places the word for past times at the end of the build
initially points to the opening letter of the word before it

parts.note: sometime as an adjective means former, once

explanation.surface: A schoolchild spotted out late, just after nine on a Thursday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sometime' means former (a sometime actor), and the clue's 'after' puts it at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A sixth-former is a pupil in the final two years of a British secondary school, aged sixteen to eighteen.

clue.text: Horse covered in spangles obscuring head and tail

indicators.note: hiding both ends of a word means its first and last letters vanish

parts.note: spangles are sequins, so covered in them is sequined

explanation.surface: A circus horse dressed in sparkly trappings that hide its head and tail.
explanation.walkthrough: Trim the first and last letters from SEQUINED to leave EQUINE.
explanation.definitionFit: Equine is the adjective and noun for animals of the horse family, so a horse is an equine.

clue.text: Is unfaithful by supporting cardinal

indicators.note: in a down entry, supporting puts the first word below the second

parts.note: a cardinal number, such as two
by as in multiplication: three by four

explanation.surface: A churchman propping up a cardinal is quietly being disloyal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cardinal' suggests a churchman; here it is a counting number. 'By' is multiplication.
explanation.definitionFit: To two-time a partner is to cheat on them by secretly seeing someone else.

clue.text: Permissible to have left off pants

indicators.note: the word left is itself to be left off, so its usual abbreviation is dropped from the longer word

explanation.surface: Is it acceptable to go about without trousers?
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang 'pants' means rubbish, very poor, so it is an adjective here, not underwear.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang uses pants to mean dreadful or of poor quality, which is what awful means.

clue.text: Bomb for delivery by Royalists?

parts.note: surface reading: an explosive device that someone is to deliver; setter's reading: a huge sum (a bomb, in British slang) paid by loyal supporters to free their captured monarch

explanation.walkthrough: In British slang 'costs a bomb' means costs a fortune. Royalists paying to deliver (free) their captive king pay a huge ransom.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for an enormous sum, from the money once demanded to release captured monarchs.

clue.text: Mass of algae sent far? All wrong

indicators.note: letters that are all wrong are in the incorrect order and must be rearranged

explanation.surface: A clump of seaweed has been sent a long way, and something has gone badly amiss.
explanation.walkthrough: Fallen star is a folk name for jelly-like blobs of algae (Nostoc) once thought to drop from meteors.
explanation.definitionFit: The gelatinous colonies of the alga Nostoc that appear on lawns after rain were popularly called fallen stars.

clue.text: Bound books concealing note

indicators.note: to conceal something is to hold it hidden inside

parts.note: the third note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: Hardbound volumes with a slip of paper tucked between the pages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound' looks like it describes the books; it is a noun meaning boundary.
explanation.definitionFit: A bound is a boundary or edge beyond which one cannot go, which is a limit.

clue.text: Swimming best in a French resort

indicators.note: letters that are swimming move about freely and settle in a new order

explanation.surface: The finest swimming to be had on the Riviera.
explanation.definitionFit: Antibes is a well-known seaside town on the Côte d'Azur between Cannes and Nice.

clue.text: Names in a region somehow in time related to monarch

indicators.note: somehow says the letters arrive by some unstated route, so they are rearranged

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for name, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: A list of names found in some district, dated somehow by the reign of a king.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'in' that ends the definition is part of it: the Latin phrase means 'in the year of the reign'.
explanation.definitionFit: Anno regni is Latin for in the year of the reign, used to date documents by a sovereign's years on the throne.

clue.text: Locals and others who've come up with rhyme

definitions.text: Locals and others who've come up
definitions.meaning: surface reading: residents plus some new arrivals
setter's reading: the residents and the students who have come up to university, named by a rhyming pair

explanation.walkthrough: To 'come up' is the British idiom for arriving at Oxford or Cambridge as a student; students wear gowns.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhyming phrase sets a university city's ordinary residents against its students, who once wore academic dress.

clue.text: Start on brandy then ring gong for dessert

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: a ring is round like the letter O
a gong is British slang for a medal or honour, such as the MBE

explanation.surface: Instructions for a dinner: brandy first, then sound the gong to call people in for pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gong' is British slang for an honour; the MBE (Member of the British Empire) is a common one.
explanation.definitionFit: A bombe is a frozen dessert of ice cream moulded into a dome, named for its round bomb-like shape.

clue.text: Rants and raves more than is necessary for a girl

indicators.note: the words supply more letters than the answer needs, so the surplus is trimmed away to leave a run inside

parts.note: a run of letters spanning the three words

explanation.surface: Someone ranting excessively over a girl.
explanation.definitionFit: Sandra is a common female first name, and crosswords use girl to clue any such name.

clue.text: Appropriate planting kiss on Queen

indicators.note: planting the item on top of the next word fixes it right after that word

parts.note: a cross on a letter stands for a kiss

explanation.surface: Is it fitting to plant a kiss on the Queen?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appropriate' looks like the adjective meaning fitting; it is the verb meaning to seize.
explanation.definitionFit: To annex territory is to take it over and claim it, which is to appropriate it.

clue.text: Our XI thrashed by almost all of the Dutch

indicators.note: almost the whole word means its last letter is dropped
a team that is thrashed is knocked about, so its letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Our cricket team trounced by nearly the whole of the Netherlands side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Dutch' is not the Netherlands: 'my old Dutch' is London slang for one's wife. XI is a team of eleven.
explanation.definitionFit: Uxorial means relating to a wife, from Latin uxor, and the Dutch is old Cockney slang for a wife.

clue.text: Wife of Douglas? Outspoken Salford native is she?

indicators.note: spoken out means the next words are judged by their sound when said

parts.note: Mancs is slang for people from Greater Manchester, which includes Salford

explanation.surface: Is the wife of a man called Douglas a plain-speaking woman from Salford?
explanation.walkthrough: Douglas is the capital of the Isle of Man, so a wife there is a woman of Man. Salford is next to Manchester.
explanation.definitionFit: A Manxwoman is a woman from the Isle of Man, whose capital is Douglas, so she could be a Douglas wife.

clue.text: Teacher suspended after taking money in poaching activity

indicators.note: taking something in means holding it inside

parts.note: tin is old British slang for money

explanation.surface: A teacher is suspended after being caught taking bribes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poaching' here means luring staff from rival firms, not taking game. Tin is old British slang for cash.
explanation.definitionFit: Headhunting is recruiting executives by enticing them away from other employers, which is poaching staff.

clue.text: Part of body of dead bird, perhaps: a tragic part

parts.note: a tern is one example of a bird

explanation.surface: An actor's tragic role somehow involves part of a dead bird's body.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dead' gives EX as in an ex-parrot: one that is no more.
explanation.definitionFit: The external ear is the visible outer portion of the organ of hearing, a part of the body.

clue.text: Fancy group knowing another language!

parts.note: to dig something is slang for liking it
a lot is a set or group

explanation.surface: An exclamation about a stylish group who speak a second tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' reads as an adjective or exclamation, but it is the verb: to like.
explanation.definitionFit: Diglot means bilingual, using two languages, from Greek for two tongues.

clue.text: Unexpectedly, she drove in place of Duke, historically

indicators.note: an unexpected outcome comes out differently, so the letters fall into another order

explanation.surface: Surprisingly, a woman took the wheel instead of the Duke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In place of' reads as 'instead of', but the phrase splits: 'in' is fodder and 'place of Duke' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Devonshire is the old full name of the county of Devon, and gives the title of the Duke of Devonshire.

clue.text: Way of getting back voting system one's not imagined being without

indicators.note: being outside the other letters means wrapping around them

parts.note: one is I, and the 's is is

explanation.surface: An election system that you can't simply imagine away is a means of returning to power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting back' looks like returning; here it is getting back at someone, revenge.
explanation.definitionFit: A reprisal is an act of retaliation, a way of getting back at an enemy for an injury.

clue.text: Coil on sink is security measure

indicators.note: in a down entry, one thing on another sits above it

parts.note: to sink is to go down, or down a drink

explanation.surface: A coiled hose fitted to a kitchen sink as a safety device.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sink' and 'coil' read as plumbing; they are a curl of hair and a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A lockdown confines people to a building or area, a security measure in emergencies or against disease.

clue.text: Sponsored youth who's joined performing to the gallery

indicators.note: joined to says one word is attached right after the other

parts.note: the gods are the highest gallery in a theatre

explanation.surface: A young protégé who has started playing to the gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Playing to the gallery' is the expected idiom, but the gallery is the gods, the theatre's top tier.
explanation.definitionFit: A godson is a boy for whom godparents act as sponsors at baptism, so he is a sponsored youth.

clue.text: TV show a forerunner to Six Feet Under?

definitions.meaning: a British sitcom about the grumpy retiree Victor Meldrew

definitions.text: a forerunner to Six Feet Under
definitions.note: a cryptic description of being close to death
definitions.meaning: being near death comes before being buried six feet deep

explanation.walkthrough: Six Feet Under is itself a US TV drama, so the clue reads as one series preceding another.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means near the end of life, which naturally precedes burial; it also names a BBC comedy series.

clue.text: Previously almost everyone available

indicators.note: almost the whole word means its last letter goes

explanation.surface: In the past, nearly everybody was free to help.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone on call is ready to be summoned to work at short notice, and so available.

clue.text: Being still a teenager maybe means stress

definitions.note: read as under score, under twenty
definitions.meaning: a teenager is under a score, under twenty years old
to emphasise, as with a line under a word

explanation.surface: A remark that adolescence is a stressful time.
explanation.walkthrough: A score is twenty, so a teenager is 'under score'.
explanation.definitionFit: To underscore a point is to emphasise it, literally by drawing a line beneath the words, so it means to stress.

clue.text: Essential element of old bomb soldiers sometimes guard

parts.note: the V-1 flying bomb of the Second World War
to mind something is to watch over it

explanation.surface: Part of an old wartime bomb that soldiers sometimes stand guard over.
explanation.walkthrough: The TA (Territorial Army) is Britain's part-time volunteer force, hence soldiers only 'sometimes'.
explanation.definitionFit: Vitamin D is a nutrient the body must have for healthy bones, one of the essential elements of diet.

clue.text: Nice cataract on rocks producing a lot of water

indicators.note: rocks as a verb means shakes violently, so the letters are tossed into a new order

explanation.surface: A pretty waterfall tumbling over rocks makes quite a torrent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On rocks' looks like one phrase; 'on' is fodder and 'rocks' is the verb that shakes it all up.
explanation.definitionFit: The Antarctic or Southern Ocean surrounds Antarctica, an immense body of water.

clue.text: Grounds for learning about politician's motives

parts.note: an MP is a Member of Parliament; the possessive just ties him to what follows
uses as in purposes or ends

explanation.surface: Reasons for finding out what drives a politician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grounds' suggests reasons; here it means land.
explanation.definitionFit: Campuses are the grounds and buildings of universities and colleges, places of learning.

clue.text: Curious article about Belgian province

indicators.note: turning about means facing the opposite direction

parts.note: rum is British for odd or curious

explanation.surface: An odd piece of writing about a region of Belgium.
explanation.definitionFit: Namur is a province in the south of Belgium, named after its capital city.

clue.text: Noble element shielding a French linesman

indicators.note: shielding something means surrounding it for protection

parts.note: argon is one of the noble gases

explanation.surface: An aristocrat protects a French line judge at a tennis match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Linesman' suggests sport; it means a writer of lines of verse.
explanation.definitionFit: Louis Aragon was a French poet and novelist, so a writer of verse lines: a French linesman.

clue.text: Young journalist sending spy after Pope

indicators.note: after places the word for spy at the end of the build

parts.note: Adrian IV, the only English pope, among others of that name
a mole is a spy planted inside an organisation

explanation.surface: A cub reporter dispatches an informant to follow the Pope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Journalist' means a keeper of a journal: the teenage diarist of Sue Townsend's comic books.
explanation.definitionFit: Adrian Mole is Sue Townsend's fictional teenage diarist, so a youngster keeping a journal.

clue.text: Wryly amusing press piece oddly ignored

parts.note: to press clothes is to iron them

indicators.note: ignoring the odd-numbered letters keeps only the even ones

parts.note: second and fourth letters of piece

explanation.surface: A newspaper article that was strangely overlooked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Press piece' suggests journalism; press is the verb for ironing.
explanation.definitionFit: Ironic humour is wry, saying the opposite of what is meant or noting cruel twists of fate.

clue.text: Announcement about girl provided, that is, by parent

explanation.surface: A father puts out a notice about his daughter.
explanation.definitionFit: A classified ad is a short paid notice in a newspaper's small-ads section, a type of announcement.

clue.text: Rope: highly unusual symbol

indicators.note: unusual means not in the normal form, so the letters take another order

explanation.surface: A rope that is highly unusual is something of a sign.
explanation.definitionFit: A hieroglyph is a picture character in writing systems such as ancient Egyptian, a written symbol.

clue.text: Tip from spear below finished off graduate

indicators.note: in a down entry, below places the weapon underneath the degree holder

parts.note: a lance is a long spear

explanation.surface: A useful hint from a spearman on how to defeat a scholar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tip' looks like advice or a point; it is the verb, to topple.
explanation.definitionFit: To overbalance is to lose balance and tip over, so tip in the sense of toppling.

clue.text: Singular, blue twinkling effect used in film

parts.note: a mo is a moment, as in the twinkling of an eye

explanation.surface: An odd blue shimmer used as a special effect on screen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twinkling' suggests a sparkle; it is 'in a twinkling', an instant.
explanation.definitionFit: Slo-mo is slow motion, the technique of showing filmed action slower than real time.

clue.text: Is seeing TV commercial the wrong way

indicators.note: going the wrong way means travelling backwards

explanation.surface: Watching a television advert from the wrong angle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seeing' is romantic: if someone is seeing a person, they date them.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who dates a person is going out with them romantically, which is also called seeing them.

clue.text: Council meeting habitual early birds might enjoy?

definitions.meaning: the imperial assembly at Worms in 1521 where Luther was condemned

definitions.note: describes the phrase read literally: a menu of worms
definitions.meaning: the early bird catches the worm, so worms would be its regular food

explanation.walkthrough: Worms is a German city; a diet is an assembly of the Holy Roman Empire.
explanation.definitionFit: The Diet of Worms was the 1521 imperial assembly that outlawed Luther, and literally a habitual menu of worms.

clue.text: Remote land specially prepared for nut producer

indicators.note: something specially prepared has been made over, so these letters are reworked

explanation.surface: Faraway soil readied to grow a nut crop.
explanation.definitionFit: The almond tree bears the almond, so it is a tree that yields nuts.

clue.text: Jack and I, solicitor general and girl, drink to celebrate

parts.note: to jack up is to raise
the Roman numeral I is one

explanation.surface: Two people, a lawyer and a young woman, have a celebratory drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jack' looks like a name; it is the verb, as when jacking up a car.
explanation.definitionFit: To raise one's glass is to lift it in a toast, drinking to mark an occasion.

clue.text: Token fix affected point nearest people

indicators.note: letters that are affected have been altered, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A superficial repair has changed which spot is closest.
explanation.definitionFit: Next of kin are a person's closest relatives, the people nearest in blood or marriage.

clue.text: Good the writer's keen on humour?

parts.note: the writer is the setter, I, and the 's here is have
being into something is being keen on it

explanation.surface: A writer asks whether a good one is fond of comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Humour' looks like a noun for comedy; it is the verb, to indulge.
explanation.definitionFit: To humour someone is to go along with their wishes to keep them happy, which is to give in to them.

clue.text: Items associated with the Pope in the public arena

parts.note: a papal bull is a formal decree
the Fisherman's Ring is the Pope's signet

explanation.surface: Papal regalia on show in a public place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Items' covers two papal things at once: the bull and the ring. A bullring is an arena for bullfights.
explanation.definitionFit: A bullring is an arena for bullfights, an open space for public spectacle.

clue.text: Food container for one with British beef

explanation.surface: A food carton meant for a single portion of British beef.
explanation.definitionFit: An egg box is a carton made to hold eggs, a container for food.

clue.text: Scot's drunk small dram and promises to pay

parts.note: a tot is a small measure of spirits

explanation.surface: A Scotsman, tipsy on a little whisky, writes out a string of debts.
explanation.definitionFit: Stotious is Scottish and Irish slang for very drunk, so a Scot's word for intoxicated.

clue.text: Girl's inducement to hurry once

parts.note: a sop is something given to pacify or bribe
hie is an archaic verb meaning hasten

explanation.surface: A girl's incentive to get a move on in the old days.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Once' marks an old word: hie, to hurry.
explanation.definitionFit: Sophie is a female first name, and crosswords clue any such name as girl.

clue.text: One may be off school gathering intelligence

indicators.note: gathering means drawing something in to hold

explanation.surface: Someone skipping school to go and collect information.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One may be off' sounds like a truant; it describes a light switch, which may be on or off.
explanation.definitionFit: A switch is a device turned on and off, so one example of something that may be off.

clue.text: See one at bridge very close to the ground

parts.note: the four bridge players are called North, South, East and West

explanation.surface: Look at someone standing on a bridge just above the earth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bridge' is the card game, whose seats are named by compass points.
explanation.definitionFit: Lowest is the superlative of low, so it means nearest of all to the ground.

clue.text: Why dwell on old, inaccurate description of some companies?

indicators.note: inaccurate means not in the correct form, so the letters must be put right

explanation.surface: Questioning why anyone would linger over an old, wrong account of certain firms.
explanation.definitionFit: A wholly-owned subsidiary is a company whose entire share capital belongs to a parent firm.

clue.text: Writing material evidently having run out, grunts

explanation.surface: A writer who has used up their ink lets out a grunt.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as '0 inks': with zero ink left, 'evidently' run out.
explanation.definitionFit: Oinks are the grunting noises a pig makes, so grunts in the farmyard sense.

clue.text: Liqueur that turned up gold

indicators.note: in a down entry, turned up means read from bottom to top

parts.note: yon is a dialect word for that one over there

explanation.surface: A drink that happens to be found alongside some gold.
explanation.definitionFit: Noyau is a brandy liqueur flavoured with fruit kernels such as apricot or peach stones.

clue.text: Overheard wine-drinker's declared preference for area of UK

indicators.note: something overheard is caught by ear, so only the sound counts

parts.note: a drinker choosing white wine over red

explanation.surface: An eavesdropper picks up what a wine drinker says they want.
explanation.definitionFit: The Isle of Wight is an island county off the south coast of England, an area of the UK.

clue.text: Bore counted on taking time out

indicators.note: taking the abbreviation for time out of a word removes that letter once

parts.note: to tot up is to count

explanation.surface: A tedious person relied on taking a break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bore' looks like a dull person; it is the past tense of bear, to carry.
explanation.definitionFit: To tote is to carry, so toted is the past tense matching bore, from bear.

clue.text: Pitcher and barrel in Greek embassy emptied

parts.note: a tun is a large cask

indicators.note: an emptied word has lost its contents, leaving only its outer letters

parts.note: first and last letters of Greek
first and last letters of embassy

explanation.surface: A jug and a cask sit inside a Greek embassy that has been cleared out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pitcher' is not a jug or baseball player: it is something that sets pitch, a tool for tuning instruments.
explanation.definitionFit: A tuning key, or tuning hammer, turns the pins of a piano or harp to set pitch, so it is a pitcher.

clue.text: Note that Saxon king has entered Burgundy perhaps

indicators.note: having entered something means being inside it

parts.note: second note of the sol-fa scale
Edwin, an Anglo-Saxon king of Northumbria

explanation.surface: A message that an Anglo-Saxon ruler has invaded Burgundy.
explanation.walkthrough: Burgundy looks like the French region; it is the wine made there.
explanation.definitionFit: Burgundy is a wine from that French region, typically a red made from Pinot Noir, so an example.

clue.text: Right oven for pan

parts.note: an oast is a kiln for drying hops

explanation.surface: Choosing the correct oven to suit a cooking pan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pan' sounds like kitchenware; it is the verb meaning to criticise harshly.
explanation.definitionFit: To pan a play or film is to criticise it severely, which is to roast it.

clue.text: One past it, but still in possession of pulse, audibly

indicators.note: audibly says what follows is judged as it is heard

parts.note: a pulse is an edible seed such as a bean

explanation.surface: An old-timer who is past it but still has a heartbeat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pulse' is the heartbeat in the surface; in the wordplay it is the bean family.
explanation.definitionFit: A has-been is someone whose time of success or fame is over, someone past it.

clue.text: Drastically affect completed objective

parts.note: time is up when it is completed

explanation.surface: A finished goal has a big impact.
explanation.definitionFit: To upend is to turn upside down, figuratively to disrupt or overturn something radically.

clue.text: Sporting attendance dropped around a Northern town

parts.note: the gate is the number of spectators at a match

indicators.note: around says one word wraps round the next

parts.note: to shed is to drop or cast off

explanation.surface: The crowd at a match has fallen off around a northern club.
explanation.walkthrough: In British sport the 'gate' is the attendance at a match.
explanation.definitionFit: Gateshead is a town in north-east England on the Tyne, opposite Newcastle.
